newsitem.title: BOSNIA: World Bank aid includes Serbs for first time.
newsitem.headline: World Bank aid includes Serbs for first time.

text.p: Bosnia's collective presidency and the World Bank signed credit agreements on Thursday that will channel substantial reconstruction funds to Serb-controlled territory for the first time.
The chairman of the three-member presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, signed credit agreements worth $32 million which will provide post-war aid for the country's Moslem-Croat and Serb territories.

"These three credits are very noteworthy because they cover all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina," Rory O'Sullivan, head of the World Bank mission in Bosnia, told reporters. "They cover activities in both entities."
The World Bank credits, the first agreed with a newly-elected central government, lay the foundation for three projects assisting hospitals, small businesses and industry.
The Serbs will receive about a third of the total credits under the deal, which was signed in a brief ceremony in Sarajevo on Thursday.
The peace treaty preserves Bosnia as single state comprised of autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.

Bosnia's Serb republic has received only an estimated two percent of international aid since the war ended in November 1995, largely because the hardline nationalist Serb leadership boycotted a donors conference last year.
Serb leaders declined to be represented as part of a Bosnian delegation and wanted separate representation for their autonomous territory.
But since a new central government was formed after elections in September, the Serbs have joined in talks with donors and attended a recent conference as part of a unifed Bosnian delegation.
Western powers, hoping to persuade the Serbs to cooperate with the peace process, have also quietly decided to increase aid to the Serb side, diplomats say.

The move has sparked a debate about how best to ensure Serb authorities comply with terms of the peace treaty, with critics warning that the financial assistance may only reward a recalcitrant leadership.
International donors were still taking a more cautious attitude towards aid to the Serb side, O'Sullivan told Reuters.
"Many donors are watching events in (the Serb republic) to determine the level of support they will provide," he said.
The World Bank planned to offer two other loans to Bosnia in March covering forestry and education projects.

An international donors conference for Bosnia is scheduled for March 5 but the event may have to be postponed if the inter-ethnic government fails to adopt a reform package proposed by the International Monetary Fund.

Before holding the confernce, many donors want the cabinet, or Council of Ministers, to approve draft laws proposed by the IMF on a single central bank, a single currency and government budgets, diplomats said.
